guideline_text: Define a high-level information security policy approved by top management that sets the organization's approach to managing information security and reflects business strategy, legal and regulatory requirements, and current and projected risks and threats. The policy should state the definition of information security, objectives, guiding principles, commitments and assignment of responsibilities, and be supported at a lower level by topic-specific policies (e.g. access control, cryptography, backup). Policies should be communicated to and acknowledged by relevant personnel and interested parties, and reviewed at planned intervals and when significant changes occur, taking management reviews and audits into account.

Define and allocate information security roles and responsibilities in accordance with the information security policy and topic-specific policies. Assign responsibilities for protection of assets, execution of specific security processes, risk management activities including acceptance of residual risk by risk owners, and the use of assets by all personnel. Individuals may delegate tasks but remain accountable; each area of responsibility and its authorization levels should be documented, and role-holders should be competent and kept up to date.

Separate conflicting duties among different individuals so that no single person can execute conflicting activities alone (e.g. initiating, approving and executing a change; requesting, approving and implementing access rights; developing and administering production systems). Determine which duties require segregation and consider the possibility of collusion when designing controls. Where segregation is impractical, especially in small organizations, apply compensating controls such as monitoring, audit trails and management supervision, and take care with role-based access to avoid granting conflicting roles.

Management should visibly support the information security policy, procedures and controls, and ensure personnel are briefed on their security roles before being granted access, provided with role-based expectations and guidelines, and required to comply with the policies. Management should ensure personnel achieve an appropriate level of awareness, maintain necessary skills through ongoing education, and comply with terms and conditions of employment. Where practicable, provide a confidential channel for reporting security violations (whistleblowing) and allocate adequate resources and time for implementing security processes and controls.

Specify when and by whom relevant authorities (e.g. law enforcement, regulatory and supervisory bodies) should be contacted, and how identified information security incidents should be reported in a timely manner. Use these contacts also to stay informed about the current and upcoming expectations of the authorities, such as applicable information security regulations.

Consider membership of special interest groups, security forums and professional associations to improve knowledge of best practices, keep the understanding of the security environment current, and receive early warnings of alerts, advisories and patches on attacks and vulnerabilities. Such membership provides access to specialist advice, enables sharing of information on new technologies, threats and vulnerabilities, and offers suitable liaison points when handling information security incidents.

Collect and analyse information about existing and emerging threats across strategic (changing threat landscape), tactical (attacker methodologies, tools and technologies) and operational (specific attacks and technical indicators) layers. Threat intelligence should be relevant, insightful, contextual and actionable, produced through defined objectives, vetted internal and external sources, and collection, processing, analysis and sharing. Integrate the resulting intelligence into risk management processes, technical preventive and detective controls (e.g. firewalls, IDS, anti-malware) and security testing, and share it with other organizations on a mutual basis.

Integrate information security into project management for all project types regardless of size or discipline. Require that security risks are assessed and treated early and periodically throughout the project life cycle, that security requirements (including application security and IP compliance) are addressed early, and that risk treatment progress and effectiveness are reviewed and tested. Define and allocate security responsibilities and authorities to specific roles, and determine security requirements by considering the information involved, its classification and protection needs, authentication and access requirements, and legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual obligations.

Identify the organization's information and other associated assets, determine their importance and maintain an accurate, up-to-date inventory (which may be a set of dynamic inventories for information, hardware, software, VMs, facilities and personnel), keeping it accurate through regular reviews or automated updates. Classify each asset in line with the classification of its associated information and record its location as appropriate. Assign ownership of each asset to an individual or group; the owner is responsible for proper management across the whole life cycle, ensuring assets are inventoried, classified, protected, subject to acceptable-use and access rules, and securely handled and removed from the inventory when disposed of.

Make personnel and external users aware of the security requirements for protecting and handling the organization's information and associated assets, and hold them responsible for their use of information processing facilities. Establish and communicate a topic-specific policy on acceptable use that states expected and unacceptable behaviours, permitted and prohibited uses, and any monitoring performed. Draw up acceptable-use procedures for the full information life cycle in line with classification, covering access restrictions, records of authorized users, protection of copies, storage per manufacturer specifications, clear marking of media and authorized disposal and deletion methods.

Formalize the employment change or termination process to include the return of all physical and electronic assets issued to or entrusted to personnel and interested parties. Where individuals use their own equipment or purchase organization equipment, ensure relevant information is traced, transferred to the organization and securely deleted, and document and transfer any important operational knowledge held by the person. Prevent unauthorized copying of relevant information (e.g. intellectual property) during the notice period, and clearly identify and document assets to be returned such as endpoint devices, portable storage, specialist equipment, authentication hardware and physical copies of information.

Establish and communicate a topic-specific policy on information classification, taking account of confidentiality, integrity and availability needs and legal requirements. Owners of information should be accountable for classification, which can be determined by the level of impact that compromise would have; each level should have a meaningful name and the scheme should be applied consistently across the organization. Include conventions for classification and criteria for periodic review, update classifications as value and sensitivity change over the life cycle, and, when sharing information externally, agree procedures to interpret and map classification levels between organizations.

Develop procedures for labelling information and associated assets in all formats that reflect the classification scheme established in 5.12, with labels that are easily recognizable and guidance on where and how they are attached. Procedures may define where labelling is omitted, how to label information on electronic or physical media, and how to handle cases where labelling is not possible; techniques include physical labels, headers and footers, metadata, watermarking and rubber stamps. Use metadata for digital information to enable identification, management, searching and automated handling decisions, make personnel aware of labelling procedures, and ensure sensitive or critical system output carries an appropriate classification label.

Establish and communicate a topic-specific policy on information transfer, with rules, procedures and agreements that reflect the classification of the information and, for transfers with third parties, transfer agreements including recipient authentication. For all transfer types, include controls against interception, unauthorized access, copying, modification, misrouting and destruction (e.g. cryptography), traceability and non-repudiation, identification of contacts, incident responsibilities and retention and disposal rules. Address specific measures for electronic transfer (e.g. malware protection, correct addressing, stronger authentication over public networks), physical media transfer (e.g. authorized couriers, tamper-evident packaging, logs) and verbal transfer (e.g. not holding confidential conversations in public places).

Have owners of information and associated assets determine access control requirements, and define and communicate a topic-specific policy on access control that considers which entities need which access, application security, physical access, the need-to-know principle and classification, restrictions on privileged access, segregation of duties, legal obligations and logging. Implement access control rules by mapping appropriate access rights and restrictions to relevant entities (human or technical), using roles to simplify management. Ensure consistency between access rights and information classification and physical perimeter needs, account for all connection types in distributed environments, and consider factors relevant to dynamic access control.

Manage the full life cycle of identities so that each identity assigned to a person is linked to a single person for accountability, shared identities are permitted only where necessary and subject to approval and documentation, and identities for non-human entities have segregated approval and independent oversight. Disable or remove identities in a timely manner when no longer required, avoid duplicate identities mapped to the same entity within a domain, and keep records of significant events concerning identity and authentication information use and management. Have a supporting process to handle changes to identity information, and where third-party identities are used, ensure they provide the required trust level and that associated risks are treated.

Manage allocation of authentication information so that temporary secrets are non-guessable, unique and changed after first use, users' identities are verified before issuing new or replacement credentials, secrets are transmitted securely, receipt is acknowledged, and vendor default authentication information is changed immediately after installation. Advise users to keep secret authentication information confidential, not to share personal passwords, to change compromised credentials immediately, and to choose strong, unique passwords. Where passwords are used, the password management system should enforce strong passwords, force change at first login, prevent reuse of previous and commonly-used passwords, not display passwords on screen, and store and transmit them in protected (hashed or encrypted) form using approved cryptographic techniques.

Operate a provisioning process for granting and revoking access rights that obtains authorization from the asset owner, considers business requirements and access control policy, enforces segregation of duties between approval and implementation, and removes rights promptly when no longer needed, especially for leavers. Use time-limited temporary access where appropriate, maintain a central record of granted rights and of changes, and modify rights when users change roles. Conduct regular reviews of physical and logical access rights (including after role changes and for privileged access), and review, adjust or remove a user's access before any change or termination of employment based on risk factors such as who initiated the change, current responsibilities and the value of accessible assets.

Establish and communicate a topic-specific policy on supplier relationships and implement processes to address the security risks of using suppliers' products and services, including cloud providers. Identify and document supplier types that can affect confidentiality, integrity or availability; define criteria to evaluate and select suppliers with adequate controls; define the information, ICT services and infrastructure suppliers may access; and assess and manage the associated risks. Monitor supplier compliance, handle non-compliance and incidents, provide awareness and training for personnel interacting with suppliers, address secure termination (de-provisioning, information handling, return of assets), and plan for continuity should a supplier become unable to provide its products or services.

Establish and document supplier agreements so both parties clearly understand their obligations to meet the identified information security requirements. Consider including a description of the information to be accessed and access methods, classification and mapping of classification schemes, legal and regulatory (including PII) requirements, obligations to implement agreed controls, acceptable use rules, authorization and removal procedures for supplier personnel, incident management requirements, training, sub-contracting provisions, screening requirements, audit rights, and third-party attestations of control effectiveness. Also address backup and disaster-recovery expectations, change management with advance notification, physical and transfer controls, and termination clauses covering records management, return of assets, secure disposal and ongoing confidentiality; maintain a register of agreements and review it regularly.

Address information security in the ICT supply chain in addition to general supplier requirements by defining security requirements for ICT product and service acquisition and requiring suppliers to propagate the organization's requirements and appropriate security practices throughout their supply chain. Request that ICT product suppliers provide information on the software components used and the security functions and configuration required for secure operation, and implement monitoring and validation (e.g. penetration testing, third-party attestations) that delivered products and services meet stated requirements. Identify critical components requiring increased scrutiny, obtain assurance that components are genuine, unaltered and traceable to their origin (using anti-tamper labels, hash verification or digital signatures), and manage component life cycle and availability risks including identifying alternative suppliers.

Regularly monitor, review and manage changes to supplier services to ensure the security terms of agreements are met, incidents are managed properly and changes do not compromise service delivery. Monitor service performance against agreements, track changes made by suppliers and to their services (e.g. new technologies, sub-suppliers, changed locations), review service reports and hold progress meetings, and conduct audits of suppliers and sub-suppliers alongside independent auditor reports. Review security event and audit records, respond to identified incidents and vulnerabilities, ensure suppliers maintain sufficient service capability and continuity plans, and assign responsibility for managing supplier relationships to a designated individual or team with adequate skills and resources.

Establish and communicate a topic-specific policy on the use of cloud services and define how the organization will manage the associated information security risks, treating this as part of its approach to managing external party services. Define relevant security requirements, selection criteria and scope, roles and responsibilities, and which controls are managed by the cloud provider versus the organization as customer, along with how to obtain assurance, handle incidents, monitor ongoing use and manage exit strategies. Review cloud service agreements to ensure they address confidentiality, integrity, availability and information handling requirements with appropriate service objectives; identify and formally accept residual risks; require advance notification of substantive customer-impacting changes; and maintain close contact with providers for mutual exchange of security information.

Establish appropriate incident management processes and determine and communicate the roles and responsibilities for carrying out incident management procedures to relevant internal and external parties. Agree incident management objectives and priorities with management, and develop and implement procedures for evaluating and classifying events, monitoring, detecting, analysing and reporting, managing incidents to conclusion including response and escalation, coordinating with interested parties, logging activities, handling evidence, root-cause analysis and identifying lessons learned. Allow only competent, trained personnel to handle incidents, provide reporting procedures with incident forms and feedback to reporters, and consider any external requirements for reporting incidents within defined timeframes (e.g. regulatory breach notification).

Agree a categorization and prioritization scheme for information security incidents, including the criteria for classifying an event as an incident and for identifying its consequences and priority. Have the point of contact assess each event using the agreed scheme, and have personnel responsible for coordinating and responding to incidents perform the assessment and decide whether an event constitutes an incident. Record the results of the assessment and decision in detail for future reference and verification.

Establish and communicate procedures for responding to information security incidents, with responses carried out by a designated, competent team. The response should include containing affected systems, collecting evidence as soon as possible, escalating as required (including crisis management and business continuity plans), and logging all response activities for later analysis. It should also cover communicating incident details to relevant parties on a need-to-know basis, coordinating with internal and external parties, formally closing and recording the incident once addressed, conducting forensic and post-incident root-cause analysis, and identifying and managing the vulnerabilities and control weaknesses that contributed to the incident.

Establish procedures to quantify and monitor the types, volumes and costs of information security incidents, and use the knowledge gained from evaluating incidents to strengthen the organization's defences. Use this information to enhance the incident management plan, scenarios and procedures, and to identify recurring or serious incidents and their causes so the risk assessment can be updated and additional controls implemented to reduce the likelihood or consequences of similar future incidents. Also use lessons learned to enhance user awareness and training by providing examples of what can happen and how to respond and avoid such incidents.

Develop and follow internal procedures for handling evidence related to information security events for disciplinary and legal purposes, taking into account the requirements of different jurisdictions to maximize admissibility. Procedures should provide instructions for the identification, collection, acquisition and preservation of evidence across different types and states of storage media and devices, ensuring records are complete and untampered, that copies are provably identical to originals, and that the source system was operating correctly. Where available, use certified or otherwise qualified personnel and tools to strengthen the value of preserved evidence, and where digital evidence crosses organizational or jurisdictional boundaries, ensure the organization is entitled to collect it.

Determine the organization's requirements for adapting information security controls during disruption and include information security requirements within business continuity management processes. Develop, implement, test, review and evaluate plans to maintain or restore the security of information for critical business processes following interruption or failure, restoring security at the required level and within the required timeframes. Implement and maintain security controls and supporting systems within business continuity and ICT continuity plans, processes to maintain existing controls during disruption, and compensating controls for those that cannot be maintained during disruption.

Treat ICT readiness as a component of business continuity management, deriving ICT continuity requirements from a business impact analysis (BIA) that assesses impacts over time, identifies prioritized activities and assigns recovery time objectives, and determines the resources (including ICT services) needed to support them along with recovery point objectives for information. Based on the BIA and risk assessment, identify and select ICT continuity strategies covering before, during and after disruption, and develop, implement and test plans to meet required availability levels and timeframes. Ensure an adequate organizational structure with competent personnel is in place, that ICT continuity plans are regularly evaluated through exercises and approved by management, and that plans specify performance and capacity requirements, RTOs and RPOs with restoration procedures.

Identify and take into account all relevant legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements when developing security policies and procedures, designing controls, classifying assets, performing risk assessments, determining roles and responsibilities, and setting supplier contractual requirements. Identify legislation relevant to the organization's information security and consider compliance in all relevant countries where it operates, uses products and services, or transfers information across jurisdictional borders, reviewing requirements regularly and documenting the specific processes and responsibilities to meet them. Give particular attention to cryptography, where specific legal restrictions on import, export, usage and mandatory access can apply (seeking legal advice as needed), and ensure contractual security requirements with clients, suppliers and insurers are addressed.

Protect intellectual property by defining and communicating a topic-specific policy on IP rights and publishing procedures for compliant use of software and information products. Acquire software only through known and reputable sources to avoid infringing copyright, maintain asset registers and proof of ownership of licences, and ensure licence limits on numbers of users or resources are not exceeded. Carry out reviews to confirm only authorized and licensed software is installed, provide procedures for maintaining licence conditions and for disposing of or transferring software, and do not duplicate, convert or extract copyrighted material (including standards, books and recordings) other than as permitted by law or licence.

Protect the authenticity, reliability, integrity and usability of records over time by issuing guidelines on their storage, handling, chain of custody and disposal that prevent manipulation, and by drawing up a retention schedule defining records and their retention periods in line with legal, regulatory and business requirements. Categorize records into types (e.g. accounting, transaction, personnel, legal) each with retention periods and allowable storage media, considering their information security classification, and choose storage systems that allow retrieval within an acceptable timeframe and format. Where electronic storage is used, ensure records remain accessible throughout the retention period despite technology change, retain any cryptographic keys and programs needed to decrypt archived records, and follow manufacturer recommendations while allowing for possible media deterioration.

Establish and communicate a topic-specific policy on privacy and protection of PII, and develop and implement procedures for preserving privacy and protecting PII, communicating them to all parties involved in processing. Ensure compliance with the procedures and all relevant legislation and regulations through appropriate roles, responsibilities and controls, often best achieved by appointing a person responsible (such as a privacy officer) to guide personnel, service providers and other parties on their responsibilities and the specific procedures to follow. Address responsibility for handling PII in light of relevant legislation and regulations, and implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect PII.

Have processes for management to plan and initiate periodic independent reviews of the organization's approach to managing information security, including the information security policy, topic-specific policies and other controls, assessing opportunities for improvement and the need for change. Carry out reviews using competent individuals who are independent of the area under review (e.g. internal audit, an independent manager or an external specialist) and outside its line of authority, and report the results to the management that initiated them and, where appropriate, to top management, maintaining records. Where reviews find the approach inadequate, management should initiate corrective actions, and additional independent reviews should be considered when laws change, significant incidents occur, the business changes, or security controls change significantly.

Have managers and service, product or information owners identify how to review that the security requirements in the information security policy, topic-specific policies, rules, standards and regulations are met, considering automated measurement and reporting tools for efficient regular review. Where non-compliance is found, managers should identify its causes, evaluate the need for corrective action, implement appropriate corrective actions, and review those actions to verify effectiveness and identify any remaining deficiencies. Record the results of reviews and corrective actions and maintain the records, report results to those performing independent reviews, and complete corrective actions in a timely manner appropriate to the risk, addressing progress at the next review if not yet completed.

Prepare documented operating procedures for operational activities associated with information security, particularly where an activity must be performed consistently by many people, is performed rarely, is new and presents risk, or is being handed over to new personnel. Procedures should specify responsible individuals; secure installation and configuration of systems; processing and handling of information; backup and resilience; scheduling and interdependencies; handling of errors and exceptional conditions; support and escalation contacts; media handling; and restart and recovery procedures. Also cover management of audit trails, log and video monitoring information and monitoring of capacity, performance and security; review and update procedures when needed, authorize changes to them, and manage systems consistently using the same procedures, tools and utilities where feasible.

Perform background verification checks on all personnel (full-time, part-time and temporary), including through contractual requirements where individuals are contracted via suppliers, handling candidate information in line with applicable legislation and informing candidates where required. Where permitted, checks may include satisfactory references, verification of the curriculum vitae, confirmation of academic and professional qualifications, independent identity verification, and more detailed checks (e.g. credit or criminal records) for critical roles. For information security roles ensure the candidate has the necessary competence and can be trusted, define criteria and limitations for verification, apply mitigating controls where verification cannot be completed in time, and repeat checks periodically according to the criticality of the role.

Ensure the contractual obligations for personnel take into account the information security policy and relevant topic-specific policies, and clarify matters such as confidentiality or non-disclosure agreements to be signed before access is granted, legal responsibilities and rights (e.g. copyright and data protection), responsibilities for classification and management of assets, handling of information received from interested parties, and actions to be taken if security requirements are disregarded. Communicate security roles and responsibilities to candidates during the pre-employment process and ensure personnel agree to terms and conditions appropriate to their level of access. Review the terms and conditions when laws, regulations or policies change, and, where appropriate, ensure relevant responsibilities continue for a defined period after employment ends.

Establish an information security awareness, education and training programme aligned with the organization's policies and procedures and the information and controls to be protected, delivering it periodically and to new personnel or those moving to roles with different security requirements, and assessing understanding to test effectiveness. The awareness programme should make personnel aware of their responsibilities and how to discharge them, be scheduled regularly, build on lessons learned from incidents, use varied channels (e.g. campaigns, e-learning, briefings), and cover management commitment, applicable rules and obligations, personal accountability, basic procedures such as event reporting and baseline controls, and contact points for advice. Provide role-specific education and training for technical teams so they can configure and maintain required security levels, acquiring missing skills and keeping knowledge up to date.

Do not initiate the disciplinary process without prior verification that a security policy violation has occurred. Provide a formal, graduated disciplinary process that takes into account the nature and gravity of the breach and its consequences, whether it was intentional or accidental, whether it is a first or repeated offence, and whether the violator was properly trained, and that considers relevant legal, statutory, regulatory, contractual and business requirements. Use the process also as a deterrent to discourage personnel and other interested parties from violating the information security policy, topic-specific policies and procedures, recognizing that deliberate violations can require immediate action.

Define which information security responsibilities and duties remain valid after termination or change of employment, such as confidentiality of information, protection of intellectual property and other knowledge, and any obligations contained in confidentiality agreements, and contain these in the individual's terms and conditions of employment, contract or agreement. Manage a change of responsibility or employment as the termination of the current role combined with the initiation of the new one, and identify and transfer to another individual any security roles and responsibilities held by a person who leaves or changes roles. Establish a process to communicate changes and operating procedures to personnel, other interested parties and relevant contacts such as customers and suppliers, and apply the process to external personnel such as suppliers as well.

Use confidentiality or non-disclosure agreements with legally enforceable terms to protect confidential information, applicable to both personnel and interested parties, with terms determined by the type of information handled, its classification, use and permissible access. When identifying requirements, consider a definition of the information to be protected, the expected duration of the agreement (including cases requiring indefinite confidentiality), required actions on termination, the responsibilities of signatories, ownership of information and intellectual property, permitted use, audit and monitoring rights, and the process for notifying and reporting unauthorized disclosure. Also address the return or destruction of information at termination and actions on non-compliance, take account of the applicable jurisdiction, and review the requirements periodically and when changes occur.

Issue a topic-specific policy on remote working that defines the conditions and restrictions for personnel working outside the organization's premises. Consider the physical security of the remote site, rules and mechanisms for the remote environment (e.g. lockable cabinets, clear-desk and disposal rules, event reporting), communications security requirements based on the sensitivity of information and systems, the threat of unauthorized access by others at the site or in public places, the use of home and public networks, and protection measures such as firewalls, malware protection and secure authentication including multi-factor for remote access. Provide suitable equipment and storage, define permitted work and the classification of information that may be held, train remote workers and support staff, enable device screen locks, location tracking and remote wipe, and provide for backup, audit and security monitoring, and revocation of access and return of equipment when remote working ends.

Make all personnel and users aware of their responsibility to report information security events as quickly as possible to prevent or minimize the effect of incidents, and ensure they know the reporting procedure and the point of contact, keeping the reporting mechanism as easy, accessible and available as possible. Consider reporting situations such as ineffective security controls, breaches of confidentiality, integrity or availability, human errors, non-compliance with policies or standards, breaches of physical security, unauthorized system changes, malfunctions or anomalous behaviour, access violations, vulnerabilities and suspected malware. Advise personnel and users not to attempt to prove suspected vulnerabilities, since testing can be interpreted as misuse, damage systems, corrupt digital evidence and result in legal liability for the individual.

Define physical security perimeters and the siting and strength of each in accordance with the security requirements of the assets they protect. Ensure perimeters for buildings or sites containing information processing facilities are physically sound with no gaps or easy break-in points: exterior roofs, walls, ceilings and flooring should be of solid construction, external doors suitably protected with control mechanisms such as bars, alarms and locks, and doors and windows locked when unattended, with external protection for windows and consideration of ventilation points. Alarm, monitor and test all fire doors on the perimeter in conjunction with the walls so they provide the required level of resistance and operate in a failsafe manner.

Control access points such as delivery and loading areas and isolate them from information processing facilities where possible. Restrict site and building access to authorized personnel with provision, review and revocation of authorizations; maintain and protect an access logbook or audit trail; and implement access-management mechanisms such as access cards, biometrics or two-factor authentication, with a monitored reception area and visible identification for personnel and visitors. Authenticate and record visitors, grant them access only for specific authorized purposes and supervise them; and secure delivery and loading areas by restricting access, designing them so deliveries can be handled without access to other parts of the building, and inspecting and registering incoming deliveries for hazardous materials and tampering.

Site critical facilities to avoid access by the public, and where applicable keep buildings unobtrusive with minimal indication of their purpose, avoiding obvious signs inside or outside that identify the presence of information processing activities. Configure facilities to prevent confidential information or activities from being visible or audible from the outside, considering electromagnetic shielding as appropriate. Do not make directories, internal telephone books or online-accessible maps that identify the locations of confidential information processing facilities readily available to unauthorized persons.

Monitor physical premises with surveillance systems such as guards, intruder alarms, video monitoring (e.g. CCTV) and physical security information management software, managed internally or by a monitoring service, and continuously monitor access to buildings housing critical systems to detect unauthorized access or suspicious behaviour. Install video monitoring to view and record access to sensitive areas, and install and periodically test contact, sound or motion detectors to trigger intruder alarms covering all external doors and accessible windows, with unoccupied areas alarmed at all times. Keep the design of monitoring systems confidential, protect them from unauthorized access and disabling, place the alarm control panel in an alarmed zone with tamperproof mechanisms, test the system regularly, and take account of local laws including data protection when monitoring personnel and retaining recordings.

Perform risk assessments to identify the potential consequences of physical and environmental threats before beginning critical operations at a site and at regular intervals, implement necessary safeguards and monitor changes to threats, obtaining specialist advice on managing risks from fire, flood, earthquake, explosion, civil unrest and other natural or human-caused disasters. Take account of the physical location and construction, including local topography (elevation, bodies of water, fault lines) and urban threats such as areas prone to unrest, crime or terrorism. Based on the risk assessment, implement appropriate controls such as early fire detection and suitable suppression, early flood detection and water pumps, protection against electrical surges, and random inspections for explosives or weapons at sensitive facilities.

Apply the security measures for working in secure areas to all personnel and cover all activities taking place there. Make personnel aware of the existence of, or activities within, a secure area only on a need-to-know basis, avoid unsupervised work in secure areas for both safety and to reduce the chance of malicious activity, and physically lock and periodically inspect vacant secure areas. Do not allow photographic, video, audio or other recording equipment (such as cameras in endpoint devices) unless authorized, appropriately control the carrying and use of endpoint devices in secure areas, and post emergency procedures in a readily visible or accessible manner.

Establish and communicate a topic-specific policy on clear desk and clear screen. Lock away sensitive or critical business information (on paper or electronic media), ideally in a safe or secure furniture, when not required, especially when the office is vacated; protect endpoint devices with key locks when unattended; and leave devices logged off or protected by a user-authenticated screen and keyboard lock, with automatic timeout or logout configured. Have originators collect printouts immediately (ideally using printers with authentication), securely store and dispose of documents and removable media containing sensitive information, provide rules for pop-ups on screens, clear sensitive information from whiteboards when no longer needed, and conduct a final sweep when vacating facilities to ensure assets are not left behind.

Site equipment to minimize unnecessary access into work areas and avoid unauthorized access, and carefully position facilities handling sensitive data to reduce the risk of information being viewed by unauthorized persons. Adopt controls to minimize the risk of physical and environmental threats such as theft, fire, explosives, smoke, water, dust, vibration, chemical effects, electrical and communications interference, electromagnetic radiation and vandalism, and establish guidelines for eating, drinking and smoking near facilities. Monitor environmental conditions such as temperature and humidity, apply lightning protection to buildings and incoming power and communications lines, use special protection methods (e.g. keyboard membranes) in industrial environments, protect equipment processing confidential information against information leakage via electromagnetic emanation, and physically separate facilities managed by the organization from those it does not manage.

Require management authorization for the use of devices that store or process information outside the organization's premises, including organization-owned and BYOD devices, and protect them accordingly. Do not leave off-premises equipment and media unattended in public or unsecured places, observe manufacturers' instructions for protection, maintain a chain-of-custody log when equipment is transferred between individuals (securely deleting information that does not need to be transferred), and require authorization and records for removal of equipment and media. Protect against viewing information in public (e.g. shoulder surfing), implement location tracking and remote wipe, and for permanently installed off-premises equipment (such as antennas and ATMs) apply physical security monitoring, protection against physical and environmental threats, tamper-proofing and logical access controls appropriate to the location's risk.

Manage removable storage media through a topic-specific policy communicated to all who use or handle them, requiring authorization and records for media removed from the organization, storing all media securely according to their classification and protecting them against environmental threats per manufacturer specifications. Use cryptographic techniques where confidentiality or integrity is important, transfer information to fresh media before degradation, store multiple copies of valuable information on separate media, enable removable media ports only where there is an organizational reason, and monitor transfers of information to such media. Establish procedures for secure reuse or disposal proportional to the sensitivity of the information, securely deleting or destroying media that held confidential information, identifying items requiring secure disposal, selecting suitable disposal suppliers, logging disposals, and considering the aggregation effect when accumulating media for disposal.

Protect equipment from power failures and other disruptions caused by failures in supporting utilities (e.g. electricity, telecommunications, water, gas, sewage, ventilation and air conditioning). Ensure utility-supporting equipment is configured, operated and maintained per manufacturer specifications, appraise utilities regularly for their capacity to meet business growth, and inspect and test them regularly to ensure proper functioning, raising alarms to detect malfunctions where necessary. Where necessary, provide multiple feeds with diverse physical routing, keep utility-supporting equipment on a separate network and connect it to the internet only when needed and in a secure manner, and provide emergency lighting, communications, and clearly located emergency switches and valves, with emergency contact details recorded and available to personnel.

Protect power and telecommunications cabling carrying data or supporting information services from interception, interference or damage. Route power and telecommunications lines into facilities underground where possible or with adequate alternative protection, and segregate power cables from communications cables to prevent interference. For sensitive or critical systems, consider additional controls such as armoured conduit, locked rooms or boxes and alarms at inspection and termination points, electromagnetic shielding, periodic technical sweeps and physical inspections for unauthorized devices, controlled access to patch panels and cable rooms, and use of fibre-optic cables. Label cables at each end with sufficient source and destination detail to enable identification and inspection, and seek specialist advice on managing risks from cabling incidents.

Maintain equipment in accordance with the supplier's recommended service frequency and specifications, and implement and monitor a maintenance programme. Ensure only authorized maintenance personnel carry out repairs, keep records of all suspected and actual faults and of all preventive and corrective maintenance, and apply appropriate controls when equipment is scheduled for maintenance, subjecting maintenance personnel to confidentiality agreements and supervising on-site work. Authorize and control access for remote maintenance, apply off-premises security measures where equipment containing information is taken away for maintenance, comply with insurance requirements, inspect equipment before returning it to operation to confirm it has not been tampered with and functions properly, and apply secure disposal or re-use measures where equipment is to be disposed of.

Verify equipment to determine whether it contains storage media prior to disposal or re-use, and for media containing confidential or copyrighted information either physically destroy it or destroy, delete or overwrite the information using techniques that make the original non-retrievable rather than the standard delete function. Remove labels and markings that identify the organization or indicate the classification, owner, system or network prior to disposal, including before reselling or donating. Consider removing security controls such as access controls or surveillance equipment at the end of a lease or when moving out of premises, taking into account the lease agreement to restore the facility, the risk of leaving sensitive information for the next tenant, and the ability to reuse the controls at the next facility.

Establish a topic-specific policy on secure configuration and handling of user endpoint devices, communicated to all relevant personnel, covering the information and classification levels devices may handle, device registration, physical protection, restriction of software installation, software update requirements, rules for connecting to networks, access controls, storage encryption, malware protection, remote disabling and wiping, and backups. Enforce these recommendations through configuration management or automated tools where possible, and consider whether sensitive information should only be accessed but not stored on devices. Make users aware of the security requirements and their responsibilities (e.g. logging off, protecting devices from unauthorized use and theft, and using care in public places), and for personal (BYOD) devices address separation of personal and business use, remote wiping, intellectual property and software licensing, and establish secure procedures for wireless connections.

Control the allocation of privileged access rights through an authorization process in accordance with the topic-specific policy on access control. Identify users needing privileged access for each system, allocate rights on an event-by-event basis to competent individuals based on the minimum needed for their roles, maintain an authorization process and a record of all privileges allocated, and define requirements for expiry of privileged rights. Ensure users are aware when they are in privileged mode, apply stronger authentication for privileged access, regularly review whether users still qualify for their privileges, avoid generic administration IDs where possible, grant temporary privileged access only for the time needed (e.g. break-glass procedures), log all privileged access, and use privileged identities only for administrative tasks rather than day-to-day activities such as email and web access.

Restrict access to information and other associated assets in accordance with the established topic-specific policies. Do not allow access to sensitive information by unknown or anonymous identities, provide configuration mechanisms to control access in systems, applications and services, control which data can be accessed by a particular user and which identities have which type of access (read, write, delete, execute), and provide physical or logical controls to isolate sensitive applications and data. For high-value sensitive information, consider dynamic access management techniques that provide granular, real-time control over who can access information, during what period and in what way, protecting it throughout its life cycle by requiring authentication and appropriate credentials, restricting access by time, using encryption, defining printing permissions, recording access and use, and raising alerts when misuse is detected.

Strictly control access to source code, associated items (such as designs, specifications and test plans) and development tools, preferably by controlling central storage in a source code management system, with read and write access differentiated by role. Provide broad read access to internal or external code repositories where appropriate, but restrict write access to privileged personnel or designated owners. Manage access to program source code and libraries per established procedures, grant read and write access based on business need to address risks of alteration and misuse, update source code and grant access only under change control procedures and after appropriate authorization, provide access through controlled developer tools rather than direct repository access, hold program listings in a secure environment, maintain an audit log of all access and changes, and, where source code is to be published, consider additional integrity controls such as digital signatures.

Choose an authentication technique appropriate to the classification of the information to be accessed to substantiate the claimed identity of users, software, messages and other entities, using methods stronger than passwords (such as digital certificates, smart cards, tokens or biometrics) and multi-factor authentication for critical systems, combined where appropriate with context-based factors such as unusual location, device or time. Invalidate compromised biometric information and provide an alternative technique. Design log-on procedures to minimize the risk of unauthorized access by not displaying sensitive system information or help messages until log-on completes, warning that only authorized users may access, validating log-on only on completion of all input, protecting against brute-force attempts, logging successful and unsuccessful attempts, raising alerts on potential breaches, not displaying or transmitting passwords in clear text, and terminating inactive sessions and restricting connection duration for high-risk applications.

Identify capacity requirements for information processing facilities, human resources and other facilities, taking into account the business criticality of the systems and processes concerned, and apply system tuning and monitoring to ensure and improve availability and efficiency. Perform stress tests to confirm sufficient capacity is available to meet peak performance requirements, and put detective controls in place to indicate problems in due time. Base projections of future capacity on new business and system requirements and current and projected trends, giving particular attention to resources with long procurement lead times or high costs, and have managers monitor the utilization of key resources to identify and avoid potential limitations. Provide sufficient capacity by increasing capacity (e.g. new hardware or cloud computing with its elasticity and scalability) or by reducing demand (e.g. deleting obsolete data, decommissioning systems, or optimizing processes), and consider a documented capacity management plan for mission-critical systems.

Base protection against malware on malware detection and repair software combined with security awareness and appropriate access and change management controls, recognizing that detection software alone is usually inadequate. Implement rules and controls that prevent or detect unauthorized software (e.g. application allowlisting) and use of known malicious websites, reduce exploitable vulnerabilities, conduct regular automated validation of software and data, and install and regularly update malware detection and repair software to scan data, email and attachments, downloads and webpages, placing tools using defence-in-depth across gateways, endpoints and servers. Protect against malware introduced during maintenance, implement a controlled process for temporarily disabling protection, prepare business continuity plans including online and offline backups for recovery from attacks, isolate high-consequence environments, provide user awareness and training, and gather information about new malware from qualified and reputable sources.

Maintain an accurate asset inventory (including software vendor, name, versions, deployment state and responsible persons) as a prerequisite for managing technical vulnerabilities, and identify vulnerabilities by defining roles and responsibilities, identifying information resources to maintain awareness, requiring suppliers to support vulnerability reporting, using vulnerability scanning tools, and conducting penetration tests. Provide a public point of contact and reporting procedures for receiving vulnerability reports, and consider bug bounty programs and information sharing. Evaluate identified vulnerabilities to determine the associated risks and required response, implement a software update management process to install approved patches (testing and validating updates before installation and addressing high-risk systems first), and where no update is available consider workarounds, disabling affected services, additional access controls, virtual patching or increased monitoring. Keep an audit log of all steps, monitor and evaluate the process, and align it with incident management, with cloud provider responsibilities defined in the cloud service agreement.

Define and implement processes and tools to enforce secure configurations for hardware, software, services and networks for both newly installed and operational systems over their lifetime, with roles, responsibilities and procedures to control all configuration changes. Define standard secure configuration templates using publicly available guidance and considering the level of protection needed, and review and update them periodically as new threats, vulnerabilities or versions arise, addressing measures such as minimizing privileged identities, disabling unnecessary identities, functions and services, restricting powerful utility programs, synchronizing clocks, changing vendor default authentication information, and invoking inactivity time-outs. Record established configurations and maintain a secure log of all configuration changes following the change management process, and monitor configurations regularly with system management tools, comparing actual configurations against target templates and addressing any deviations by automatic enforcement or manual analysis and corrective action.

Do not keep sensitive information longer than required in order to reduce the risk of undesirable disclosure, and when deleting information select a deletion method (e.g. electronic overwriting or cryptographic erasure) in accordance with business requirements and relevant laws, recording the results as evidence and obtaining evidence of deletion from service suppliers where used. In accordance with the data retention policy, delete sensitive information when no longer required by configuring systems to securely destroy it, deleting obsolete versions, copies and temporary files, using approved secure deletion software or certified disposal services, and using disposal mechanisms appropriate for the storage media type (e.g. degaussing magnetic media). Where cloud services are used, verify the provider's deletion method is acceptable and automate deletion where applicable, protect sensitive information by removing auxiliary storage and memory before equipment leaves the premises, and keep an official record of deletion to help analyse any possible information leakage.

Where protection of sensitive data such as PII is a concern, hide the data using techniques such as data masking, pseudonymization or anonymization, verifying that data has been adequately pseudonymized or anonymized and considering all elements of the sensitive information so that individuals cannot be identified indirectly. Additional masking techniques include encryption requiring a key, nulling or deleting characters, varying numbers and dates, substitution, and replacing values with their hash. When implementing masking, grant users access only to the minimum required data, design mechanisms for obfuscation where some data should not be visible for certain records, and account for legal or regulatory requirements. When using masking, pseudonymization or anonymization, consider the level of strength according to the usage of the data, access controls, agreements and restrictions on usage, prohibiting collation with other information to re-identify the PII principal, and keeping track of the processed data provided and received.

Reduce the risk of data leakage by identifying and classifying information to protect against leakage, monitoring channels of leakage (e.g. email, file transfers, mobile devices and portable storage), and acting to prevent information from leaking (e.g. quarantining emails containing sensitive information). Use data leakage prevention tools to identify and monitor sensitive information at risk of unauthorized disclosure, detect disclosure (e.g. uploads to untrusted cloud services), and block user actions or network transmissions that expose sensitive information. Determine whether to restrict users' ability to copy, paste or upload data to services, devices or media outside the organization, allow the data owner to approve any required export and hold users accountable, address taking screenshots through terms of use, training and auditing, and protect backed-up sensitive information using encryption, access control and physical protection.

Establish a topic-specific policy on backup addressing data retention and security requirements, and provide adequate backup facilities so that all essential information and software can be recovered following an incident, failure or loss of media, developing and implementing backup plans accordingly. When designing the plan, produce accurate records and documented restoration procedures, reflect the business requirements (e.g. recovery point objective) and criticality in the extent and frequency of backups, store backups in a safe and secure remote location with appropriate physical and environmental protection, and protect backups by encryption according to risk. Regularly test backup media and restoration procedures against required restoration times, ensuring critical systems can be recovered fully, take backups of information, applications and systems held in cloud services, and consider deleting information from backup media once its retention period expires, taking legislation into account.

Identify requirements for the availability of business services and information systems, and design and implement systems architecture with appropriate redundancy to meet them, introducing redundancy by duplicating information processing facilities in part or entirety. Plan and implement procedures for activating redundant components and facilities, establishing whether they are always active or activated automatically or manually in an emergency, and ensure redundant components provide the same security level as the primary ones. Put mechanisms in place to alert the organization to failures and enable continued availability while facilities are repaired or replaced, and consider measures such as contracting multiple suppliers, redundant networks, geographically separate mirrored data centres, redundant power supplies, parallel load-balanced software instances and duplicated components; test redundant systems, preferably in production mode, to ensure failover works as intended.

Determine the purpose, content and protection requirements for logs and document them in a topic-specific policy on logging, including in each event as applicable user IDs, system activities, dates and times, device identity and location, and network addresses and protocols. Consider logging events such as successful and rejected access attempts, configuration changes, use of privileges and utility programs, files accessed, alarms from the access control system, and creation, modification or deletion of identities, and synchronize time sources across systems to enable correlation. Protect logs so that users, including privileged users, cannot delete or de-activate logs of their own activities, guarding against unauthorized changes and storage overflow using techniques such as cryptographic hashing and append-only or read-only recording, and de-identify logs sent to vendors and apply privacy protection where logs contain sensitive data. Perform log analysis to identify unusual or anomalous activity and indicators of compromise, supported by monitoring activities and threat intelligence, and subject suspected and actual incidents to further investigation.

Determine the monitoring scope and level in accordance with business and security requirements and relevant laws, and maintain monitoring records for defined retention periods. Include in the monitoring system inbound and outbound network, system and application traffic, access to systems and networking equipment, critical or admin-level configuration files, logs from security tools (e.g. antivirus, IDS/IPS, web filters, firewalls, DLP), event logs, verification that executed code is authorized and untampered, and resource usage and performance. Establish a baseline of normal behaviour (considering normal and peak utilization and usual access times, locations and frequency) and monitor against it for anomalies such as unplanned process termination, malware-associated activity, known attack characteristics, unusual system behaviour, unauthorized access or scanning, and bottlenecks. Use continuous monitoring tools able to handle large data volumes and provide real-time alerting tuned to the baseline to minimize false positives, dedicate trained personnel to respond to alerts, communicate abnormal events, and establish procedures to respond to positive indicators and to identify and address false positives.

Document and implement external and internal requirements for time representation, reliable synchronization and accuracy, which can arise from legal, statutory, regulatory, contractual, standards and internal monitoring needs. Define a standard reference time for use within the organization and consider it for all systems (including building management, entry and exit systems) that can aid investigations, using a clock linked to a radio time broadcast from a national atomic clock or GPS as the reference for logging systems to provide a consistent, trusted date and time source for accurate time-stamps. Use protocols such as NTP or PTP to keep all networked systems synchronized with the reference clock, optionally using two external time sources to improve reliability and managing any variance, and where clock synchronization is difficult across multiple cloud or cloud and on-premises services, monitor each service's clock and record the difference to mitigate discrepancy risks.

Restrict and tightly control the use of utility programs capable of overriding system and application controls. Limit their use to the minimum practical number of trusted, authorized users; use identification, authentication and authorization procedures including unique identification of the person using the program; and define and document authorization levels and require authorization for ad hoc use. Do not make utility programs available to users who have access to applications on systems requiring segregation of duties, remove or disable all unnecessary utility programs, apply at least logical segregation of utility programs from application software (and, where practical, separate their network communications from application traffic), limit their availability (e.g. only for the duration of an authorized change), and log all use of utility programs.

Securely manage changes and installation of software on operational systems by having only trained administrators perform updates upon appropriate management authorization, ensuring only approved executable code and no development code or compilers is installed, and installing and updating software only after extensive and successful testing. Update corresponding program source libraries, use a configuration control system for all operational software and documentation, define a rollback strategy before implementing changes, maintain an audit log of all updates, and archive old software versions with the required information as a contingency measure. Base decisions to upgrade on business requirements and the security of the release, maintain vendor-supplied and open source software at a supported and current level while considering the risks of relying on unsupported software, monitor externally supplied software and packages for unauthorized changes, grant supplier access only when necessary and with authorization while monitoring their activities, and enforce strict least-privilege rules on which software users can install.

Implement controls to ensure the security of information in networks and protect connected services from unauthorized access. Consider the type and classification of information the network supports, establish responsibilities and procedures for managing networking equipment, maintain up-to-date network documentation and configuration files, separate operational responsibility for networks from ICT system operations where appropriate, and establish controls to safeguard the confidentiality and integrity of data passing over public, third-party or wireless networks. Apply appropriate logging and monitoring, coordinate network management to apply controls consistently, authenticate systems on the network, restrict and filter connections (e.g. using firewalls), harden network devices, segregate network administration channels from other traffic, temporarily isolate critical subnetworks if the network is under attack, disable vulnerable protocols, and apply appropriate security controls to virtualized networks including software-defined networking.

Identify and implement the security measures necessary for particular network services, such as security features, service levels and service requirements, whether provided by internal or external network service providers, and ensure providers implement these measures. Determine and regularly monitor the provider's ability to manage agreed services securely, agree the right to audit, and consider third-party attestations demonstrating appropriate security measures. Formulate and implement rules on the use of networks and network services covering which networks and services may be accessed, authentication and authorization requirements, technological controls to protect access, the means used to access networks (e.g. VPN or wireless), user context attributes, and monitoring of use. Consider security features of network services including authentication, encryption and network connection controls, the technical parameters for secured connections, caching parameters, and procedures to restrict access to services or applications where necessary.

Manage the security of large networks by dividing them into separate network domains and separating them from the public network, choosing domains based on levels of trust, criticality and sensitivity, along organizational units, or a combination, using physically different or logical networks. Define the perimeter of each domain well, and where access between domains is allowed, control it at the perimeter using a gateway such as a firewall or filtering router, basing the criteria for segregation and the access allowed on an assessment of each domain's security requirements in accordance with the access control policy. Give wireless networks special treatment because of their poorly defined perimeter, adjusting radio coverage for segregation and, for sensitive environments, treating all wireless access as external and routing it through a gateway before granting access to internal systems, and segregate guest wireless access from personnel access with at least the same restrictions.

Reduce the risk of personnel accessing websites containing illegal information or known to contain viruses or phishing material, typically by blocking the IP address or domain of the websites concerned, using browser or anti-malware technologies that do this automatically or can be configured to do so. Identify the types of websites to which personnel should or should not have access, and consider blocking websites with an upload function unless permitted for valid business reasons, known or suspected malicious websites (e.g. distributing malware or phishing content), command and control servers, malicious websites identified from threat intelligence, and websites sharing illegal content. Before deploying the control, establish and keep up to date rules for safe and appropriate use of online resources, and train personnel on secure use of online resources including the rules, the contact point for security concerns, the exception process for legitimate access to restricted resources, and not overriding browser advisories that report a website is insecure.

When using cryptography, follow a topic-specific policy on cryptography that sets the general principles for protecting information, identifies the required level of protection and information classification to establish the type, strength and quality of algorithms, and defines the use of cryptography for information on mobile devices and media and in transit, the approach to key management, and roles and responsibilities. Adopt approved standards, algorithms, cipher strengths and usage practices, take into account regulations and national restrictions on cryptography and cross-border flows of encrypted information, and consider the impact of encryption on content-inspection controls. Base key management on agreed standards, procedures and secure methods for generating, issuing, distributing, storing, changing, revoking, recovering, backing up, archiving and destroying keys, along with logging and auditing key management activities and setting activation and deactivation dates; protect all keys against modification, loss and unauthorized use or disclosure, and physically protect key-generation and storage equipment.

Treat secure development as a requirement for building secure services, architectures, software and systems, and address it by separating development, test and production environments, providing guidance on security throughout the software development life cycle, and defining secure coding guidelines for each programming language used. Incorporate security requirements in the specification and design phases and security checkpoints in projects, conduct system and security testing such as regression testing, code scanning and penetration tests, use secure repositories for source code and configuration, and apply security in version control. Ensure required application security knowledge and training and developers' capability to prevent, find and fix vulnerabilities, address licensing requirements, and where development is outsourced obtain assurance that the supplier complies with the organization's rules for secure development.

Identify and specify application security requirements, usually determined through a risk assessment and developed with the support of information security specialists. Depending on the application's purpose, requirements should include as applicable the level of trust in the identity of entities, identification of the type and classification of information processed, segregation and level of access to data and functions, resilience against malicious attacks (e.g. protection against buffer overflow or SQL injection), legal and regulatory requirements, privacy needs, protection of confidential information in processing, transit and at rest, encryption of communications, input and output controls, and error message handling. For applications offering transactional services between the organization and a partner, additionally consider the level of trust in each party's identity and the integrity of exchanged information, authorization processes for key transactional documents, and confidentiality, integrity and non-repudiation of transactions; and for electronic ordering and payment applications, consider maintaining confidentiality and integrity of order and payment information, avoiding loss or duplication of transactions, and securely storing transaction details.

Establish, document and apply secure system engineering principles to information system engineering activities, designing security into all architecture layers (business, data, applications and technology), analysing new technology for security risks and reviewing designs against known attack patterns. Secure engineering principles should include analysis of the full range of security controls required, the capabilities of controls to prevent, detect or respond to security events, controls required by particular business processes, and where and how controls are applied and work together, taking account of the need to integrate with a security architecture and technical security infrastructure, the organization's capability, and current good practice. Apply security architecture principles such as security by design, defence in depth, least privilege, fail securely and least functionality, conduct security-oriented design reviews, harden systems, and consider zero trust principles such as assuming breach, never trust and always verify, end-to-end encryption and dynamic access control; apply the principles to outsourced development through contracts and review them regularly to keep them effective against new threats.

Establish organization-wide processes to provide good governance for secure coding, establishing and applying a minimum secure baseline extended to cover third-party and open source software components, and monitoring real-world threats and up-to-date advice to guide secure coding principles through continual improvement. Before coding, address organization-specific expectations and approved principles, common coding defects, configuration of development tools to enforce secure code, developer qualification, secure design and architecture including threat modelling, and use of controlled development environments. During coding, use secure coding practices specific to the languages and techniques in use, secure programming techniques such as peer review and test-driven development, structured programming, documentation and removal of defects, and prohibit insecure techniques such as hard-coded passwords; conduct testing including static application security testing. After code is operational, securely package and deploy updates, handle reported vulnerabilities, log and review errors and suspected attacks, and protect source code against unauthorized access and tampering, managing external libraries and vetting reused components.

Thoroughly test and verify new information systems, upgrades and new versions during development, making security testing an integral part of testing for systems or components and conducting it against a defined set of functional or non-functional requirements. Security testing should include testing of security functions (e.g. user authentication, access restriction and use of cryptography), secure coding and secure configurations of operating systems, firewalls and other security components, with test plans covering a detailed schedule, inputs and expected outputs, evaluation criteria and decisions on further action. Leverage automated tools such as code analysis tools and vulnerability scanners and verify remediation of security defects, performing initial tests by the development team for in-house developments followed by independent acceptance testing including code review, vulnerability scanning and penetration testing; for outsourced development and purchased components follow an acquisition process with contracts addressing security requirements, and perform testing in an environment matching production as closely as possible.

Where system development is outsourced, communicate and agree requirements and expectations, and continually monitor and review whether the delivery of outsourced work meets them across the entire external supply chain. Consider licensing agreements, code ownership and intellectual property rights, contractual requirements for secure design, coding and testing practices, provision of the threat model to external developers, and acceptance testing for the quality and accuracy of deliverables. Also obtain evidence that minimum acceptable levels of security and privacy capabilities are established and that sufficient testing has been applied to guard against malicious content and known vulnerabilities, establish escrow agreements for source code, secure the contractual right to audit development processes and controls, define security requirements for the development environment, and take account of applicable legislation such as on protection of personal data.

Identify and implement the level of separation between production, testing and development environments necessary to prevent production problems. Adequately separate development and production systems, operating them in different domains (e.g. separate virtual or physical environments); define, document and implement rules and authorization for deploying software from development to production; test changes in a testing or staging environment before applying them to production and avoid testing in production except in defined and approved circumstances; keep development tools inaccessible from production when not required; display environment identification labels to reduce error; and avoid copying sensitive information into development and testing environments unless equivalent controls are provided. Protect development and testing environments through patching and updating tools, secure configuration, access control, monitoring of change and secure monitoring, and backups, and prevent a single person from making changes to both development and production without prior review and approval, applying detailed logging and real-time monitoring in exceptional situations.

Ensure the introduction of new systems and major changes to existing systems follow agreed rules and a formal process of documentation, specification, testing, quality control and managed implementation, with management responsibilities and procedures to control all changes. Document and enforce change control procedures to protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information across the entire system development life cycle from early design through all maintenance, integrating ICT infrastructure and software change control where practicable. The change control procedures should include planning and assessing the potential impact of changes considering all dependencies, authorization of changes, communication to interested parties, testing and acceptance of tests, implementation including deployment plans, emergency and contingency considerations including fall-back procedures, maintaining records of changes, and ensuring operating documentation, user procedures and ICT continuity and recovery plans are updated as necessary to remain appropriate.

Select test information to ensure the reliability of test results and the confidentiality of the relevant operational information, and do not copy sensitive information (including PII) into development and testing environments. When copies of operational information are used for testing, whether the test environment is in-house or on a cloud service, apply the same access control procedures as those applied to operational environments, require separate authorization each time operational information is copied to a test environment, and log the copying and use of operational information to provide an audit trail. Protect sensitive information by removal or masking if used for testing, properly delete operational information from the test environment immediately after testing is complete to prevent unauthorized use, and securely store test information used only for testing purposes to prevent tampering that could otherwise lead to invalid results.

Plan and agree audit tests and assessments involving operational systems to minimize their impact on business processes. Agree audit requests for access to systems and data with appropriate management, and agree and control the scope of technical audit tests, limiting them to read-only access to software and data; where read-only access is not available, have an experienced administrator with the necessary rights execute the test on behalf of the auditor. Before allowing access, establish and verify the security requirements (e.g. antivirus and patching) of the devices used for access; only allow access other than read-only for isolated copies of system files, deleting them when the audit is complete or protecting them if they must be retained; identify and agree requests for special or additional processing such as running audit tools; run audit tests that can affect availability outside business hours; and monitor and log all access for audit and test purposes.
